title: Perforated peptic ulcer
seen_note: 436F — exactly like previous" (pain, vomiting, diffuse tenderness, NSAID history — history & exam not asked)
scenario: A patient presented with epigastric pain and vomiting; history given in the scenario; asked to examine and manage. 435

A young man with epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, using NSAIDs for headache (simulated patient). Old exam Abdominal pain after eating → diagnosed with PUD → returns with very severe pain to the ER. 437A · 438F · 439B
Epigastric pain radiating to the right hypochondrium. 439A

imgs.cap: Erect chest X-ray — air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum)

a: Pain (SOCRATES): sudden severe epigastric pain → generalised, worse with movement.
Associated: N/V, dysphagia, regurgitation, haematemesis, melaena, diarrhoea; constitutional symptoms.
Risk factors: NSAIDs/aspirin, H. pylori, smoking, severe burn/stress, bariatric surgery, known PUD.
PMH, drugs, previous surgery/endoscopy/NGT, family & social history.
qs.why: Sudden severe epigastric pain that becomes generalised is the story of perforation; NSAIDs, H. pylori and smoking are the main risk factors to ask about.
hist: Sudden severe epigastric pain → generalised, worse with movement
Sudden onset is typical of perforation; spread to the whole abdomen and pain on moving mean generalised peritonitis.
Nausea, vomiting, haematemesis, melaena
Show associated upper GI pathology — an ulcer can bleed as well as perforate.
Dysphagia, regurgitation
Help exclude oesophageal causes in the differential.
Diarrhoea and constitutional symptoms
Help exclude other differentials (gastroenteritis, malignancy).
NSAIDs/aspirin, H. pylori, smoking
The main causes of peptic ulcer disease.
Severe burn or stress, bariatric surgery, known PUD
Stress (Curling) ulcers, marginal ulcers after bypass and a known ulcer all raise the probability.
PMH, drugs, previous surgery/endoscopy/NGT
Previous instrumentation can cause perforation; drugs and comorbidities matter for anaesthesia and surgery.

a: Start with general look (patient in severe pain, lying still) and vitals.
Palpate away from the pain; if the patient refuses because of pain, say so — if told to proceed, continue gently.
Findings: epigastric/diffuse tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound tenderness.
Finish by saying you would do a PR exam and examine the external genitalia; summarise.
qs.why: Peritonitis gives a board-like abdomen with guarding and rebound; examine gently from away from the pain and always mention completing with PR and genital exam.

a: Perforated peptic ulcer, acute pancreatitis, acute cholecystitis, inferior MI, ruptured AAA, lower- lobe pneumonia (also gastritis, appendicitis, liver disease).
qs.why: Upper abdominal catastrophes and the "medical" mimics (inferior MI, lower-lobe pneumonia, ruptured AAA) must be on the list because they present the same way.

a: Bloods: CBC, U&E, LFT, coagulation profile, amylase (pancreatic enzymes), cardiac enzymes, cross-match.
Imaging: erect chest X-ray.
qs.why: Amylase excludes pancreatitis, troponin excludes MI; an erect CXR is the quickest test for free gas from a perforated viscus.

qs.q: The patient comes with very severe pain — what will you do?
a: Erect chest X-ray.
qs.why: Very severe sudden pain suggests perforation — an erect chest X-ray (sitting up 10 min) shows free gas under the diaphragm.

qs.q: What do you see on this X-ray?
a: Air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum).
qs.why: Free gas between the diaphragm and liver means a hollow viscus has perforated (pneumoperitoneum).

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Perforated peptic ulcer (NSAID user).
qs.why: NSAID use + sudden epigastric pain + peritonitis + free air = perforated peptic ulcer.

qs.q: How will you manage this patient?
a: ABC; NPO + NGT.
2 large-bore IV lines (14–16 G) in the antecubital fossa; draw bloods; IV fluids.
IV PPI, IV antibiotics, analgesia; Foley catheter to monitor input/output.
Laparotomy and Graham (omental) patch: close the perforation and cover it with a pedicle of omentum, then a second layer.
qs.why: Peritonitis needs resuscitation, gastric decompression, PPI and antibiotics, then surgery to close the hole — the omental (Graham) patch seals it.

qs.q: What are the differences between a perforated and a bleeding ulcer?
a: Bleeding: posterior duodenal (gastroduodenal artery), painless; endoscopy (dual therapy) → angio-embolisation or surgery if endoscopy fails.
Perforated: anterior; sudden severe pain, rebound, fever, leukocytosis; erect CXR shows free air (endoscopy contraindicated); surgery — Graham patch.
qs.why: Anterior ulcers perforate into the peritoneal cavity; posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed. Endoscopy treats bleeding, but is contraindicated in perforation.

title: Upper GI bleeding — haematemesis / variceal bleeding
scenario: A patient presented to the ER with a history of vomiting fresh blood. 430A · Archive
A patient (70 y/o) presented to the ER with upper GI bleeding and a history of weight loss. 436F · 438A Mohammed, 55, came to the ER vomiting blood — history-taking checklist station. Archive
A patient vomiting blood with a significant history of recurrent hospital admissions. 439A

imgs.cap: The marking checklist of the history station (ARC2)

qs.q: What is the urgent management in the ER?
a: ABC; look for shock (tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension, cold extremities).
2 large-bore IV cannulas (14–16 G) in the antecubital fossae; bloods: CBC with differential, U&E, LFT, coagulation profile, cross-match, hepatitis serology.
Start Ringer's lactate, then blood: PRBCs + platelets + FFP 1 : 1 : 1 (better survival than crystalloid alone); correct coagulopathy.
IV PPI; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (high risk of sepsis in cirrhotics); analgesia.
NGT (decompress the stomach), Foley catheter; monitor BP, HR, SpO₂, urine output. Then endoscopy.
qs.why: Haematemesis can kill from hypovolaemia, so resuscitation comes before diagnosis: large-bore access, bloods, balanced transfusion, PPI, and antibiotics because cirrhotic bleeders often have infection that worsens outcome.

a: Vomit: colour (bright/dark), amount, frequency; melaena.
Liver disease: yellow discoloration (jaundice), itching, pale stool, dark urine, abdominal pain/distension.
Abdominal pain or heartburn (PUD), symptoms of anaemia, constitutional symptoms (weight & appetite loss).
Risk factors for cirrhosis: alcohol, drug abuse, blood transfusion & unprotected sex (hepatitis), travel (e.g. Egypt), vaccination status (hepatitis).
Drugs: NSAIDs, anticoagulants.
qs.why: The history separates the two big causes — liver disease (variceal) and peptic ulcer — and looks for red flags (weight loss = malignancy) and the risk factors for cirrhosis.
hist: Vomit colour, amount, frequency
Fresh red blood means active, brisk bleeding; dark "coffee-ground" vomit means slower or older bleeding. Amount and frequency estimate how much blood has been lost.
Melaena
Black tarry stool means blood has passed through the gut (upper GI source) and adds to the estimate of blood loss.
Jaundice, itching, pale stool, dark urine, distension
Features of liver disease point to cirrhosis with portal hypertension, so varices become the likely source of bleeding.
Epigastric pain or heartburn
Points to peptic ulcer disease, the commonest non-variceal cause.
Symptoms of anaemia
Dizziness, fatigue, palpitations and shortness of breath show how much the bleed has affected the patient.
Weight and appetite loss
Raises suspicion of a gastric or oesophageal cancer as the bleeding source.
Alcohol, drugs, transfusion, unprotected sex, travel, vaccination
These are the risk factors for alcoholic and viral (hepatitis B/C) cirrhosis.
NSAIDs and anticoagulants
NSAIDs cause ulcers and erosions; anticoagulants make any bleed worse and must be reversed.

a: Oesophageal varices
Peptic ulcer (posterior duodenal ulcer — gastroduodenal artery), gastritis, oesophagitis Mallory–Weiss tear
Aorto-enteric fistula
Iatrogenic trauma (endoscopy, NGT, laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy)
qs.why: Upper GI bleeding arises above the ligament of Treitz: varices and peptic ulcers are commonest; Mallory–Weiss and aorto-enteric fistula are classic exam additions.

a: CBC, LFT, RFT & electrolytes, pancreatic enzymes, coagulation profile, cross-match. Upper GI endoscopy (± CT).
qs.why: Bloods measure blood loss, liver function and clotting; upper GI endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis? (checklist station)
a: Liver cirrhosis (portal hypertension → variceal bleeding).
qs.why: Signs of chronic liver disease with haematemesis point to portal hypertension and bleeding oesophageal varices.

qs.q: What is the specific (variceal) management? / How would you treat this patient?
a: 1st: endoscopy with band ligation (or sclerotherapy — more complications).
2nd: octreotide / vasopressin (terlipressin) → splanchnic vasoconstriction, ↓ portal pressure (stops ~90%); propranolol later.
Endoscopy fails or not available → balloon tamponade as a bridge (controls ~85%, re-bleeds on removal — temporary, for transfer or surgery).
Then TIPS (refractory acute bleeding, recurrent life-threatening bleeds, refractory ascites) → surgery (spleno-renal shunt) / angio-embolisation last.
qs.why: Band ligation directly controls the bleeding varix; vasoactive drugs (octreotide/terlipressin) lower portal pressure; balloon tamponade buys time; TIPS decompresses the portal system when these fail.

a: Liver transplant.
qs.why: Varices are a consequence of cirrhosis; only liver transplantation treats the underlying cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

a: Primary (never bled): non-selective β-blocker; endoscopic band ligation (serial, every 2 weeks) if β-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated.
Secondary (after the first bleed): β-blocker + serial band ligation.
qs.why: Non-selective β-blockers lower portal pressure and band ligation eradicates varices — together they reduce first bleeds and re-bleeding.

tips.t: "5 tubes": 2 IV lines, Foley catheter, NGT, endoscope. Checklist answer: "ABCs then endoscope" (terlipressin / octreotide also accepted).
439A — the doctor stressed the 2 most important questions: why was he admitted multiple times, and what was the cause and management of each admission?

a: Weight history: onset, maximum weight, recent change; BMI.
Diet (meals, snacks, sugary drinks), physical activity, sleep.
Previous weight-loss attempts (diet, drugs, bariatric surgery) and outcomes.
Complications: DM, HTN, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea (snoring, daytime sleepiness), GERD, joint pain, PCOS/infertility, depression.
Secondary causes: hypothyroidism, Cushing's, drugs (steroids, antipsychotics, insulin). Family history of obesity; social & psychological history; motivation.
qs.why: An obesity history measures the problem, looks for treatable secondary causes, lists the comorbidities that bariatric surgery improves, and records previous attempts — all needed to decide eligibility for surgery.
hist: Weight history and BMI
Onset, maximum weight and recent change show the pattern and severity; BMI classifies obesity and decides eligibility for bariatric surgery.
Diet, activity, sleep
Identify the modifiable causes that lifestyle treatment targets.
Previous weight-loss attempts
Bariatric surgery is considered after non-surgical methods have failed; a previous operation changes the plan.
Diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia
Obesity-related comorbidities that lower the BMI threshold for surgery and improve after it.
Snoring, daytime sleepiness
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea, which matters for anaesthesia.
GERD, joint pain, PCOS/infertility, depression
Other obesity complications; GERD also influences the choice of operation (sleeve can worsen reflux).
Hypothyroidism, Cushing's, steroids, antipsychotics, insulin
Secondary causes that are treated differently and must be excluded.
Family, social and psychological history; motivation
Support, eating disorders and motivation predict success and compliance after surgery.

title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
scenario: A patient presents with typical reflux symptoms (heartburn, acid regurgitation). (new case) 442F

a: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, functional dyspepsia, oesophageal motility disorder, cardiac chest pain (if atypical).
qs.why: Heartburn and regurgitation are typical of GERD, but ulcer, functional dyspepsia, motility disorders and cardiac pain can mimic it.

qs.q: What will you look for in the history and examination?
a: Typical symptoms: heartburn, regurgitation, worse after meals or lying down.
Alarm features: dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, anaemia, persistent vomiting.
Risk factors: obesity, smoking, late meals. Examination is usually normal.
qs.why: Typical symptoms allow empirical treatment; alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia) suggest cancer or complications and demand endoscopy first.

a: Empirical PPI once daily before breakfast for 4–8 weeks + lifestyle changes (weight loss, raise the head of the bed, avoid late meals).
qs.why: Without alarm features, a PPI trial plus lifestyle change is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

qs.q: The patient is not improving — what next?
a: Optimise the PPI (increase dose / check compliance); still symptomatic → upper endoscopy (OGD).
qs.why: Failure of an adequate PPI trial means the diagnosis or its complications need confirming — endoscopy.

qs.q: What are you looking for in endoscopy?
a: Oesophagitis, strictures, hiatal hernia.
qs.why: Endoscopy grades the damage (oesophagitis, stricture, Barrett's) and shows a hiatal hernia.

qs.q: Endoscopy shows complications (oesophagitis + stricture) — what next?
a: Surgical management.
qs.why: Complicated or refractory reflux despite optimal medication is the indication for anti-reflux surgery.

a: Nissen fundoplication.
qs.why: Nissen fundoplication restores the anti-reflux barrier and is the standard operation.

a: Laparoscopically; the gastric fundus is wrapped 360° around the distal oesophagus to increase LES pressure.
qs.why: Wrapping the fundus 360° around the lower oesophagus creates a high-pressure zone that acts as a valve; the hiatus is repaired at the same time.

qs.q: What are the complications of surgery?
a: Dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, recurrence of reflux.
qs.why: A wrap that is too tight causes dysphagia and inability to belch (gas bloat); a loose or slipped wrap lets reflux recur.

tips.t: Careful — most students said H. pylori eradication; that was wrong.

bonus.stem: A 20-year-old underweight woman has nausea, vomiting and early satiety. CT shows compression of the 3rd part of the duodenum between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: D. Small-bowel obstruction due to adhesions
bonus.ans: Answer: B — SMA syndrome (loss of the mesenteric fat pad after weight loss).
